sense: from a place or a person

terms.gloss: from (away from a place or a person)
terms.grammar: preposition with the ablative; ā before consonants, ab before vowels and h
evidence: Vulg. Ps. 112 (113), 3: Ā sōlis ortū ūsque ad occāsum
terms.comment: From the side of a place or a person: ā mē, from me; ā Rōmā, from the neighbourhood of Rome. Abs tē is the form of comedy and of Cicero until about 54 BC (Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: preposition with the ablative; ex before vowels and often before consonants, ē only before consonants
evidence: Sen. Ep. 35.3: venit ad nōs ex iīs quōs amāmus … gaudium
terms.comment: From inside a thing, or from among a number: see out of.

evidence: Cic. Att. 12.2.2: dē viā rēctā ad mē
terms.comment: From a place or a surface, often downward: dē viā, from the road; dē mēnsā, off the table (see off).

terms.gloss: from home, from the country; from Rome
evidence: Verg. A. 8.113–114: quī genus? unde domō?
terms.comment: Names of towns and small islands, domus and rūs take no preposition: Rōmā proficīscī, set out from Rome; domō exīre, leave the house.

phrases.latin: Ā sōlis ortū ūsque ad occāsum laudābile nōmen Dominī.
phrases.english: From the rising of the sun to its setting the name of the Lord is to be praised.

phrases.latin: jam tē vidēbō et quidem, ut spērō, dē viā rēctā ad mē
phrases.english: I shall see you soon, and, I hope, straight from the road to my house

phrases.latin: venit ad nōs ex iīs quōs amāmus etiam absentibus gaudium
phrases.english: joy comes to us from those we love, even when they are away

phrases.latin: quō tenditis? inquit; quī genus? unde domō?
phrases.english: “Where are you heading?” he said. “Who are your people? Where are you from?”
